#### **A double blow**

Easter Monday, March 26, 1951

It must’ve been 10 o'clock in the morning when Dr Anne Casey, 36, started to worry. Little Laura was in bouncing on her big pregnant belly and couldn't be stopped. Normally she'd be in with her daddy in the other room. Anne hauled herself out of bed and waddled over to the mirror-image bedroom occupied by her husband, Dr Austie Casey, 52.

Austie hadn't been in the best of health for some time and he'd already had two heart attacks. As soon as she opened the door, she let out a yelp, to the horror of the children and anyone else scattered around the house. There he was, dead to the world. He had slipped away in his sleep, painlessly she hoped.

The house was curiously empty for a festive weekend. By now, Anne had taken to the other room because she was due to have the baby any day now, and the complications were as bad as they could be. There was still hope though, even if the odds were against them. Laura Ann had been a miracle and was a ruddy two year old now, the first Rhesus baby in Ireland to survive. She got the all-important blood transfusion, a procedure that had only recently been developed in America. Austie must have had to muscle his way through his medical contacts in Dublin as he managed to pull together a team who could save the baby. The chances of survival would be even lower for subsequent babies but there was still hope. With Austie gone, however, and Anne so ill, they didn't have anyone with the clout or energy to pull together the right team for the coming birth. Alas, nine days later, in his absence, the young widow would bear a still born baby, Joseph Patrick Casey, 0, and his little body would be buried beside his father in the loose soil of the family grave.

Jane was **five** and remembers it all. How could you not? Richard was six and Michael, the eldest, was eight, his father's pride and joy, and now he would have to become the man of the house. Whenever Anne came to, she told Michael to run down and get the nanny. When no one came, Anne had to traipse down the stairs, her flock trailing behind her, to ask the maids where that aul wan was gone to. They said she was gone to Mass. The aul dragon! She's always gone to mass when she's wanted. Anne struggled back up the stairs and Michael went in with his mammy to see his father, and him there, gone.

#### **Enjoy it while you can**

The early years had been idyllic for the Casey family. The war was over, the world was opening up, and the prosperous couple had begun to galavant. Michael Augustine Casey **had long been** the Medical Officer for the county town of Dungarvan in west Waterford, along the southern coast of Ireland. Incredibly, he was also the managing director of the town's two factories, both of which he had helped set up. In recent years, he found himself and his beautiful wife travelling all around America, buying machines and visiting family in Chicago and Los Angeles. Business was booming now and the men of Dungarvan and surroundings areas had steady work, all year round, largely thanks to Austie Casey. The 1950s hadn't happened yet and the mood in Ireland was still hopeful. No sooner were the lovers back from The States and they went on a cruise to Portugal and Madeira. They had a nanny and three maids to help them raise the children, along with Granny May, Anne mother.

Soon the children would be like stray cats. With no father, their mother would be flat out as a dispensary doctor, working like a dog to keep the whole thing going, thanks to the paltry stipend she received in accordance with Austie's second will, which had been changed after one of his heart attacks. Soon enough, Austie's siblings all began to drop, some of them afflicted by the same heart condition. In ten years' time, only one of the six was still alive. **JOE?**

### **Mountain View House**

Mr and Mrs Michael Augustine Casey lived in a large Georgian house called Mountain View, on a two-acre plot just off O'Connell Street, as you head west out from the square, a few hundred metres. Despite being so close to the town centre, it feels like a country house, and, in its fine original state, it had space aplenty for a family doctor's duties by day and entertaining guests by night.

-   However, it would certainly not have been equipped to deal with the sheer number of people who wanted to pay their respects to deceased before his removal on the Tuesday evening.

<!-- -->

-   *The house has a quite formal entry hall, with a truly imposing entry port, a hefty ornate timber door in a wide, fan-lit surround with side glazing features also on the ornate side of the scale.*

-   To the right was a very long dining-room, twenty-six feet by fifteen, and it was separated by an arch from a drawing room with a huge fire place. I suspect that Austie's body would have been laid to rest

-   and there are seven bedrooms.

The finest two are at the front of the house, upstairs, with huge sash windows looking straight out at **Knockmealdown** mountain, to the admittedly north, making them slightly dreary, and lacking in restorative light energy. Outside, the house was covered all in ivy, head to toe, and around the beautiful non-original porch which has sadly been removed. The staff would have tended to the ample gardens which were walled off from the surroundings, leaving an idyllic space for Austie's young children to wander and play. They might enter in the back door

*Beyond, there’s an entry area with wood floor, and just beyond a stone floor section running the rest of the way through the rather deep property.*

The original residents, in 1815, were the Dower family, local scions of commerce and law. Eventually it would come to house the local Medical Officer and this is why it became the incongruously large home of a single man in his early thirties, Dr Michael Augustine Casey, at a time when young Anne Foley was in Ardmore, studying for the Leaving Certificate. The house came with the job, which was bad news for Anne, as Austie had never actually bought it. Instead, his money went into shares for the factory.

**Siblings**

Percy would have been the first to get to Mountain View. He was Austie's younger brother and had become is right hand man. He lived on the main street in Dungarvan and still oversaw the family business, a shop that had been owned by their father, Michael J., the much-loved champion of the town's poor, until his death in 1923, and later taken over by his equally-loved wife, Catherine, until her death in 1940. Both of them had huge funerals in the town. Together the Casey brothers set up the Glue and Gelatine factory during The War and, after Austie died, Percy would take on a lot of his responsibilities. He too would **become managing director** of Dickens Leather and would begin to build business connections abroad. Like their father, Percy would become a member of the county council before, like Austie, he would succumb to a heart attack in 1957, **aged just 50.**

The rest of them were as scattered as any large Irish family of the time. Cork, Dublin, England, America. May was married to a Dr Michael O'Shea, and they lived in his native Cork City. Joe, a highly successful accountant, had flown all the way from Los Angeles, where Austie and Anne had visited him on their tour of the States. Rennie had come from Lancashire where he worked as part of a mission among the large Irish community, although he would retire with illness and see out his days in Mountain View, later that decade.

Funeral

Dungarvan shut down on the morning of the funeral and the place was so jammed that the car couldn't move through the crowd. Despite its size, the church couldn't accommodate all the mourners and hundreds had to stand in the precincts. Everyone could attend the burial immediately afterwards as the family plot was right by the entrance to the church. The people in attendance demonstrated the remarkably wide range of activities and contacts Austie had made in a life that paralleled perfectly the Irish nation in the first half of the twentieth century. A very large number in attendance would have been patients of Austie, for whom he had worked so painstakingly and conscientiously since his appointment as the local medical officer in **1932,** after a stint in nearby Cappoquin. There were the factory staff who had carried his body to the church the night before.

After that, the gathering was a diffuse, educated bunch, many of them leaders in the newly formed republic, hailing mostly from the East and South of the country. There were Austie's medical contacts, built up first in University College Dublin, where his studies overlapped with the Revolutionary Period of 1916-23, what he would have called The Troubles. His self-confessed involvement with the IRA in both Dublin and Waterford got him involved in politics and, in particular, Fianna Fail after their establishment and rise to power. It was through these contacts that, in 1935, he could organise the establishment of a large leather factory in Dungarvan, which Minister Sean Lemass would open. Several members attended from Dail Eireann and Seanad Eireann, along with officials from all public bodies in the country. The Waterford County Council members attended en bloc, as arranged at their emergency meeting on the Tuesday.

As a board member of two factories, Austie came into contact with many members of the legal and banking professions, and other managers and directors of various industrial concerns throughout the provinces of Munster and Leinster. It was through the work of such men that Ireland tried to fashion itself as a self-sufficient state, independent of Britain and scarcely connected by trade to Europe.

Austie's involvement in Gaelic games was honoured by the President of the GAA and very large attendance from the Gaels of Waterford, namely the people of the community. **Austie played a huge role in local games.** This era was the high point of Waterford hurling and football. They won the All-Ireland in 1948 and 1949, with Dungarvan being the bulk suppliers, and the Waterfod Foot

In attendance also were also Garda and Army representatives in attendance; the latter may have gotten to know Austie through his eldest brother, Fr. Richard, who had been Head Chaplain in the army until 1948.

Dick would have surely driven down from Skerries where he had, by his energetic standards, retired into a posting as Parish Priest, a role he kept until his death in 1962. It is highly unlikely, given his profession, that he was at home for Easter when Austie died, although he certainly would continue to be a regular guest in Mountain View.

Astonishingly, Dick was the celebrant of the mass (a **Solemn Requiem and High mass**) and was joined by an enormous array of local priests, inlcluding those from the parishes of Abbeyside, Old Parish. Ardmore

-    Joe, a highly successful accountant, had flown all the way from Los Angeles, where Austie and Anne had visited him on their tour of the States. Rennie had come from Lancashire where he worked as part of a mission among the large Irish community, although he would retire with illness and see out his days in Mountain View, later that decade. Percy had stayed local although his galavanting days were about to begin as he would step into Austie's shoes before also succumbing to a heart attack in 1957. Percy also ran a shop in the middle of the town which had been owned by their father, Michael J., the much-loved champion of the town's poor, until his death in 1923, and later taken over by his equally-loved wife, Catherine, until her death in 1940. **The gathering for Austie was perhaps the largest in the town since his mother died.**

-   It's a big claim as he may not have even been the greatest leatherman to grace County Waterford in the early twentieth century – that award surely goes to Limerick's Kennedy O'Brien, who helped established tanneries in both Portlaw and Dungarvan, and elsewhere too.

    -   That honour perhaps belongs to Kennedy O'Brien, a *bona fide* leather man, who lived and breathed leather production from the age of *seventeen* when he began working in ?1907? in Ireland's last remaining big tannery.

-   But that perhaps only demonstrates the culture of Free State Eire at a time when the colonial aristocrats had been recently ousted and the industrial heartlands of the northern province had been partitioned off, leaving the body of an island without its industrious legs.

    -   The country had to bootstrap itself into a functional economic entity, led by a small, educated middle-class who would scramble to fill the new power vacuum, and **powered** by a class of labourers who were capable of hard, physical, and even noxious work.

-   Austie's biggest strength was neither on the factory floor nor in the day-to-day running of the business. He was the one who brought jobs to the people of Dungarvan, and not just seasonal work, as would have been common, but year-round work for the people of the town and countryside.
